title: Questioning Your Own Biases
keyIdea: An assumption is something you believe without checking. Everyone's brain makes quick guesses about people, often without noticing; when those guesses lean for or against someone, that is bias, and a bias you are not aware of is unconscious bias. First impressions rest on very little evidence. Confirmation bias makes you notice what fits an idea and miss what does not, and in-group bias pulls you towards people like you, even in a random group. You cannot switch bias off, but you can catch it: notice the snap thought, pause, ask what your evidence is and whether you would think the same about someone else, then check by finding out more.

kid: An assumption is something you believe without checking. We all make them. Your brain makes quick guesses to save time, often before you notice. When a quick guess leans for or against a person, that is a bias. A bias you are not aware of is called an unconscious bias.

First impressions can trick you. Kai is quiet on his first day, so you might think he is unfriendly. But he could be shy, or still learning English. One quiet day is not enough evidence. When Kai lends you a pencil and asks to play, your view should change.

Biases can grow. Once you believe an idea, you notice the things that fit it and skip the things that do not. That is confirmation bias. We also tend to favour people who seem like us, even when the group is only a sticker colour. That is in-group bias.

You cannot switch bias off, but you can catch it. Notice the snap thought and pause. Ask: what is my evidence? Would I think the same about someone else? This is called the flip test. Then check by finding out more, or by asking the person. Do it every time, not once.
adult: This topic fits the PSHE Association plan for Key Stage 2, under respectful relationships and living in the wider world. Pupils learn to spot and challenge stereotypes and assumptions. They learn to respect people who are not like them. The DfE guidance on Relationships Education asks for the same. The focus here is on checking your own thinking, not judging other people.

Useful terms: assumption, first impression, snap judgement, evidence, bias, unconscious or implicit bias, confirmation bias, in-group bias, stereotype and perspective. Confirmation bias is the habit of seeking and keeping what fits a belief; Nickerson reviewed it in 1998. In 1970 Tajfel put boys into groups for a trivial reason. They still gave their own group more points. Keep claims modest: tests that say they measure a person's hidden bias are still debated.

Common mistakes: thinking only unkind people have biases; thinking you can be free of bias just by deciding to; treating a nice assumption, such as quiet children are clever, as harmless; mixing up what someone did with a guess about who they are; and feeling so ashamed of a bias that you hide it. Be careful to show checking as a habit for life. It leads to fairer choices and more empathy.

In the lab the learner drags a guess about how friendly quiet new Kai is. Then they open four clues and move it. They tap eight things Mia did while a bossy filter fades the kind ones, and count what fits. They share ten tokens between two strangers sorted by a random sticker colour. They flip four snap thoughts to judge evidence or assumption, and put notice, pause, ask and check in order.

familyTip: Over dinner, each person shares one first impression they had about someone that turned out wrong, and what changed their mind. Then try the flip test on a headline or a TV character together.

visual.caption: Evidence or assumption? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Zara has helped tidy up after every art lesson, so she is helpful.
Tom has been on time every day this month, so he is punctual.
Priya won the last three chess games, so she is a strong player.
He is tall, so he must be good at basketball.
She is quiet, so she must be stuck-up.
They live in a big house, so they must be spoilt.
He wears glasses, so he must be clever.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: revise a first impression, see what a bossy filter hides, share tokens across random teams, flip snap thoughts, then notice, pause, ask, check.

practice.prompt: When you question your own biases, what is an assumption?
choices: Something you believe without checking
A fact you have proved
A rule the school has made
practice.hint: Think about whether you have looked for evidence or not.
practice.explain: An assumption is believed without checking. It might be right or wrong, which is why it is worth questioning.

practice.prompt: You think Mia is bossy. You notice {a} bossy things she did, but miss {b} kind things. How many things did Mia really do?
practice.hint: Add the things you noticed and the things you missed.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} things. Seeing only {a} of them is confirmation bias at work.

practice.prompt: Kai is quiet on his first day. Which thought shows you are questioning an assumption?
choices: Maybe he is shy or new. I will say hi and find out.
He is quiet, so he must be unfriendly.
Quiet people never make good friends.
practice.hint: Which thought looks for more evidence before judging?
practice.explain: Saying hi to find out tests the first impression. The other two jump from one quiet day to a fixed judgement.

practice.prompt: In a sharing game you give {a} of 10 tokens to a stranger with your own sticker colour. How many more tokens does your colour get than the other colour?
practice.hint: First find how many tokens the other colour gets, then find the difference.
practice.explain: The other colour gets 10 − {a} = {=10-a}, so your colour gets {a} − {=10-a} = {=2*a-10} more. Favouring your own random group is in-group bias.

choices: Noticing what fits your idea and missing what does not
Checking every fact very carefully
Agreeing with a friend to be kind
pool.hint: It is about which evidence your mind keeps and which it lets slip.
pool.explain: Confirmation bias means seeking and remembering what fits a belief while skipping the rest.

pool.prompt: Max was early on {n} days and late on 2 days. Someone who thinks Max is lazy remembers only the late days. How many days do they forget?
pool.hint: Which days do not fit the idea that Max is lazy?
pool.explain: They forget the {n} early days, because those do not fit the idea. That is confirmation bias.

pool.prompt: Which question best checks your own bias?
choices: Would I think the same about someone else?
How can I prove I am right?
Who agrees with me?
pool.hint: One question swaps the person to test whether the judgement is fair.
pool.explain: The flip test swaps the person. If your view would change, it rests on who they are, not what they did.

choices: Everyone does
Only unkind people
Only adults
pool.hint: Think about how every brain makes quick guesses to save time.
pool.explain: Everyone does, because every brain makes quick guesses. Being aware of them is what lets you check them.

pool.prompt: Leah judged the new boy after {n} minutes on his first day. The school day is 360 minutes. How many minutes of that day had she not seen yet?
pool.hint: Take the minutes she saw away from the whole day.
pool.explain: 360 − {n} = {=360-n} minutes she had not seen. A first impression uses very little evidence.

pool.prompt: Which thought is based on evidence?
choices: Ravi has scored in every match, so he is good at football
Ella wears glasses, so she must be clever
The new girl lives on a farm, so she will not like computers
pool.hint: Evidence is about what the person has actually done.
pool.explain: Ravi's goals are things he did. Glasses and living on a farm say nothing about being clever or liking computers.

pool.prompt: In Tajfel's experiments, boys were put into groups for a trivial reason. What did they tend to do?
choices: Give their own group more points
Share points the same with everyone
Give the other group more points
pool.hint: Think about the pull towards people on your own side.
pool.explain: They tended to favour their own group, even though the groups meant nothing. This is in-group bias.

pool.prompt: You realise you judged someone unfairly. What is the best next step?
choices: Find out more and change your view
Hide it so no one knows
Decide you are a bad person
pool.hint: Questioning a bias is a habit. What do you do once you have caught one?
pool.explain: Finding out more and changing your view fixes the unfair judgement. Hiding or shame leaves it in place.
